claims.text: HEA green bodies can be produced by 3D ink-extrusion printing from blends of Co3O4, Cr2O3, Fe2O3, and NiO powders.
Standard sintering of these oxide-derived green bodies results in significant porosity.
Standard sintering of these green bodies causes dimensional variability.
A hydrogen-rich reduction dwell at 1100–1200 K before final sintering will completely reduce the oxides, particularly Cr2O3.
Final sintering at approximately 1573 K with furnace cooling is suitable for the proposed process.
Unreduced Cr2O3 decreases contact between metallic particles and inhibits sintering.
Larger residual Cr2O3 particles act as local diffusion barriers and inhibit densification.
Eliminating residual oxides will enhance interparticle contact and make diffusion more uniform across the matrix.
Converting refractory oxide inclusions to metal before final densification removes localized diffusion barriers.
Residual refractory oxides serve as pore-forming sites.
Removing oxide-related barriers produces stronger and more uniform particle bonding during sintering.
Stronger and more uniform particle bonding improves dimensional precision.
Stronger and more uniform particle bonding improves the mechanical integrity of the components.
The sequential reduction treatment will reduce porosity to below 1%.
The baseline process has porosity above 20%.
The sequential reduction treatment will improve both strength and ductility relative to the baseline.
Incomplete Cr2O3 reduction in the baseline process causes high porosity, dimensional inaccuracies, and poor mechanical performance.
The intervention is primarily applicable to oxide-based, binder-derived green bodies and may have a different effect with pre-alloyed metallic powders.
Optimal reduction temperature and dwell time depend on alloy composition.
An improperly optimized reduction treatment may cause excessive grain growth.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis and intervention state that the proposed 1100–1200 K step will ensure complete oxide reduction, while the uncertainty field concedes that the effective temperature and time window remains undetermined and requires optimization.

The baseline broadly characterizes oxide-ink processing as producing incomplete reduction and high porosity, but cited same-system evidence reports that co-reduction and sintering of an oxide ink produced CoCrFeNi with only 0.4 ± 0.1% porosity and excellent mechanical performance.
